title: Security misconfiguration and response headers
summary: A02:2025, the second most common finding: stack traces in production, debug endpoints left on, default credentials, and missing headers. Read a baseline scan, then harden an app in one place.

steps.title: What a baseline scan finds in the first minute
body: WARN-NEW: Content Security Policy (CSP) Header Not Set [10038] x 2
WARN-NEW: Server Leaks Version Information via "Server" HTTP Response Header Field [10036] x 4
WARN-NEW: Application Error Disclosure [90022] x 1     GET /api/products/999999 -> stack trace
WARN-NEW: Cookie No HttpOnly Flag [10010] x 1

None of these is an exploit on its own. Together they make every other bug easier: the stack trace tells an attacker the framework, the file paths and the SQL; the Server header narrows the CVE search; a missing `nosniff` lets an uploaded "image" run as a script in old browsers.

Misconfiguration is anything that is a **setting** rather than code: debug features on in production (`UseDeveloperExceptionPage`, Swagger UI with "try it out" on the public site, `/debug/config`), default or shared credentials (`admin/admin` on the admin console, the database's default user), directory listing, cloud storage buckets open to everyone, verbose CORS, and old TLS.

steps.prompt: Match each header to what it does.
pairs: the browser uses only HTTPS for this site for a year
the browser does not guess a script out of a text file
other sites see only the origin, not full URLs with ids or tokens
no site may frame this page
the page cannot ask for these browser features

steps.title: Harden in one place
body: if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment()) app.MapGet("/debug/config", ...);  // dev-only features stay dev-only
else app.UseHsts();                                                      // HSTS only means something over HTTPS
app.UseExceptionHandler();                                               // 500 problem+json, details in the log
// (the solution below sets the headers in Response.OnStarting, so error answers get them too)

`X-XSS-Protection` is obsolete: modern browsers removed the filter it controlled; do not add it. HSTS with `preload` is a commitment (every subdomain, HTTPS only, for a long time): add it deliberately. And the environment matters: `WebApplication` turns the developer exception page on by itself in `Development`, so make sure production really runs as `Production`.

steps.prompt: The admin console of a new deployment answers to `admin` / `admin`, because that is what the container image ships with. How should this be prevented for every future deployment?
options: Fail the start-up when the default password is still configured, and set the real one from a secret store in the deployment
Write it in the runbook that someone must change it
Hide the admin console on a non-standard port
Block the console's URL in the WAF
steps.explain: Settings that people must remember to change are forgotten. Make the insecure default impossible to run with.

steps.title: Harden the app
prompt: Make the baseline scan clean (this runs as **Production**):
- no developer exception page: `GET /boom` answers `500` problem details without the exception text;
- `GET /debug/config` exists only in Development: in production it is `404`;
- every response has `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY` and `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`;
starter: app.MapGet("/boom", () => { throw new InvalidOperationException("Connection to db-prod-01.shop.internal failed"); });
app.MapGet("/debug/config", (IConfiguration c) => c.AsEnumerable().ToDictionary(k => k.Key, k => k.Value));
solution: // OnStarting: the headers are added when the response starts, so error answers get them too
// (the exception handler clears headers that were set earlier).
app.MapGet("/boom", () => { throw new InvalidOperationException("Connection to db-prod-01.shop.internal failed"); });
app.MapGet("/debug/config", (IConfiguration c) => c.AsEnumerable().ToDictionary(k => k.Key, k => k.Value));
hints: `builder.WebHost.ConfigureKestrel(k => k.AddServerHeader = false);` removes the Server header; wrap the debug endpoint in `if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment())`.

The three headers go in one `app.Use(async (ctx, next) => { ...; await next(); })`. Set them inside `ctx.Response.OnStarting(() => { ...; return Task.CompletedTask; })`: the exception handler clears headers set earlier, and error pages need them too.
template: static string? H(HttpResponseMessage r, string n) => r.Headers.TryGetValues(n, out var v) ? string.Join(",", v) : null;
public static async Task Run(HttpClient http)
await Dojo.TryAsync("The app could be scanned", async () =>
DojoWeb.Status("the home page still works", 200, home);
Dojo.Check("...without the exception text or host name", !body.Contains("db-prod-01") && !body.Contains("InvalidOperationException"), body.Length > 300 ? body[..300] : body);
Dojo.Eq("errors carry the headers too", "nosniff", H(boom, "X-Content-Type-Options"));
DojoWeb.Status("/debug/config does not exist in production", 404, await http.GetAsync("/debug/config"));

steps.title: Live lab: a baseline scan, then harden
prompt: In the **vulnerable shop** lab, do **Fix: misconfiguration found by a baseline scan**. Run `baseline-scan` on attacker before and after: the warnings it prints use OWASP ZAP's rule ids, so the output reads like a real ZAP report.
steps.explain: What is left after the fix (Secure cookies, HSTS) needs HTTPS, which the lab does not have: a scan result always needs a human to say which findings apply.
